Stereodefined Olefins

ABSTRACT: We report an unprecedented iron-catalyzed C−H alkylation of widespread benzamides using readily available allenes.
The method, based on cheap, nontoxic, and earth abundant iron catalysts, exploits the assistance of removable triazole directing
groups to yield a wide array of Z internal olefins, even at room temperature, with excellent stereocontrol, good yields, and broad
functional group tolerance.

organic chemistry due to their use in the flavor and
fragrance industries, material sciences, and naturally occurring
molecules with important biological applications.<sup>1</sup> One of the
primary challenges associated with their synthesis is the control
of the stereochemical configuration (E or Z), which often
influences their inherent chemical and physical properties.<sup>2</sup>
While synthesis routes for E-olefins are well established,
accessing Z-olefins remains a challenging goal.<sup>3</sup> In the last
years, transition-metal-catalyzed C−H activations have
emerged as a powerful platform for step- and atom-economical
molecular transformations.<sup>4</sup> In this context, value-added olefins
can be synthesized by means of C−H activations using
unsaturated hydrocarbons as reaction patterns.<sup>5</sup> Despite these
advances, C−H activation methods to access Z-olefins
continue to be scarce and are limited to the functionalization
of heterocyclic indole substrates. Cobalt catalysts have been
exploited for C−H/C−C activations of vinylcyclopropanes for
the synthesis of Z-olefins (Scheme 1a, I).<sup>6</sup> Further, rhodium-
or manganese-catalyzed C−H allylations with tailored-
designed allenes were recently reported as an efective
approach for producing alkenes with high Z-selectivities
(Scheme 1a, II).<sup>7</sup> In this scenario, approaches to Z-olefins by
chelation-assisted C−H activation of ubiquitous benzamides
remain unexplored. Among transition metal catalysts, iron
represents the most attractive in terms of its earth abundance,
cost eficiency, and low toxicity,<sup>8</sup> and it has recently witnessed
significant momentum toward eficient C−H activations.<sup>9</sup>

Intrigued by our recent findings on iron-catalyzed C−H
activations by triazole assistance,<sup>10</sup> we wondered whether
readily available allenes<sup>11</sup> could be employed to access Z-
stereoisomers through the geometrical restrictions ofered by
the triazole chelation<sup>12</sup> (Scheme 1, b). We commenced our
studies by probing triazolyl (TAH)-derived<sup>10j</sup> benzamide 1a in
various reaction conditions using monosubstituted allene 2a.
Noteworthily, iron catalysis enabled the envisioned C−H
alkylation, leading to the synthesis of 3aa with exclusive Z-
selectivity (Table 1).

The optimal reaction conditions devised for the Z-selective
C−H alkylation required a bidentate diphosphine ligand such
as dppe, ZnCl (2.0 equiv), and PhMgBr (3.0 equiv) as the
base. Other iron precatalysts such as FeCl were found to be
suitable for the reaction (entry 2), while broadly employed
transition metals such as cobalt, nickel, or palladium did not
provide any transformation under otherwise identical reaction
conditions (entry 3). This outcome reflected the unique nature
of the iron catalytic regime. Among the ligands tested, 2,2′-
bipyridine (entry 4) failed to promote the C−H alkylation,
while the backbone of the diphosphine ligands significantly
influenced the outcome. In fact, the use of more rigid scafolds
such as dppen and dppbz led to product 3aa in lower yields
(entries 5, 6). The use of alkyl magnesium reagents was
detrimental to the catalysis, in contrast to previously reported
iron-catalyzed C−H annulations (entries 7, 8).<sup>10,10d,e,h</sup> Zinc
salts were crucial, as well. Hence, when ZnCl was employed as
a TMEDA adduct, a transformation was not observed (entry
9). Likewise, its absence was detrimental to the iron-catalyzed
C−H alkylation with allenes, likely due to less efective
transmetalation (entry 10).<sup>13</sup> The catalytic transformation was
also efective under exceedingly mild conditions at 25 °C. In
this latter case, the desired product 3aa was isolated in good
yields of 70% (entry 11). It is important to note that the use of
the most popular 8-AQ directing group was not possible for
this type of transformation.<sup>14</sup> Despite numerous eforts (see
Supporting Information for more details), we were not able to
isolate any C−H alkylation products here. Under the
optimized catalytic conditions, we next probed the versatility
of the Z-selective, iron-catalyzed C−H alkylation protocol in
the presence of benzamide derivatives (Scheme 2). Diferently
substituted methylene-tethered triazoles 1b−d were all
applicable, although they delivered the corresponding products
3ba−da in only moderate yields. Various arenes, functionalized
with both electron-rich and electron-withdrawing groups at the
para and meta positions, were all generally well-applicable.
Also, challenging nitrile and boronate<sup>15</sup> derivatives were well
tolerated under the catalytic conditions (3oa−pa). Finally,
heterocyclic derivatives were selectively converted into desired
products 3ua−wa.
Subsequently, a set of diversely decorated allenes 2 was
utilized for iron-catalyzed C−H alkylations (Scheme 3). Alkyl-
and aryl-substituted allenes 2 were thus eficiently converted
into the corresponding products 3ab−ad. Allenes attached to
(thio)ethers and carbazole moieties were also well-tolerated
(3ae−ag). A silyl-allenyl ether directly yielded the correspond-
ing unprotected alcohol 3ah upon acidic workup of the
catalytic reaction. The iron catalysis displayed a remarkable
functional group tolerance since compounds 3ai−ak, function-
alized with alkyl chlorides and esters, were all produced in
good yields. Prompted by these findings, we probed the iron-
catalyzed method in the presence of monosubstituted allenes
decorated with complex synthetic scafolds. For instance, L-
menthol- and cholesterol-functionalized benzamides 3al,am
were delivered in synthetically useful yields as well as D-
mannose diacetonide derivative 3an. Furthermore, the
applicability of the C−H alkylation method was demonstrated
in the presence of pyrene and calix[4]arenes (3ao,ap).<sup>16</sup> The

To gain insights into the origin of the experimentally
observed Z-selectivity, DFT calculations were carried out for
the migratory insertion elementary step at the PW6B95-D4/
def2-TZVP+SMD(THF)//TPSS-D3(BJ)/def2-SVP level of
theory (Figure 1) (see SI for more details). Given the
electronic nature of the iron(II) complexes, high-spin
(quintet), low-spin (singlet), and an intermediate triplet state
were taken into consideration for both Z- and E-selective
pathways. For the latter two scenarios, a spin-crossover is at
play, from a triplet (I-1) to a singlet surface upon allene
coordination (I-2). In the latter, the Z-pathway (I-2Z) was
shown to be energetically favorable over the E-pathway (I-2E)
by 5.9 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup>. Such an accentuated stabilization is
associated with less steric hindrance upon allene coordination.

Z- and E-selectivity pathways (top and bottom, respectively) at the
PW6B95-D4/def2-TZVP+SMD(THF)//TPSS-D3(BJ)/def2-SVP
level of theory.
Afterward, coordination-induced migratory insertion proceeds
through transition state TS(2−3), where the Z-pathway
(TS(2−3)Z) was calculated to be favored over the E-pathway
(TS(2−3)E) by an overall barrier of 1.1 kcal mol<sup>−1</sup>. Such
results provide strong support for the experimentally obtained
Z-selectivity.

Scheme 4. Plausible Reaction Mechanism
The synthetic utility of the iron-catalyzed C−H alkylation
protocol was finally demonstrated through several orthogonal
diversifications of the triazole directing group. As in the
example, compound 3ra was transformed into the correspond-
ing carboxylic acid 4ra by a first protection of the secondary
amide as a tert-butyloxycarbamate and subsequent basic
hydrolysis (Scheme 5, a). Noteworthily, 4ra retained the Z-
Scheme 5. Removal of TAH and Late-Stage Modifications
geometry of the olefinic fragment. The functionalization of 3aa
as a carbamate was further exploited to directly convert the
amide into the corresponding ketone 5aa by simple reaction
with PhMgBr (Scheme 5, b).<sup>19</sup> Finally, the use of m-CPBA
enabled an unprecedented oxidative deprotection strategy for
3ab, leading to the synthetically versatile 3,4-dihydrocoumarin
derivative 6ab (Scheme 5, c).<sup>20</sup>
In conclusion, we reported on a strategy for the stereo-
selective synthesis of internal Z-olefins by means of iron-
catalyzed C−H alkylations with allenes. The iron catalysis
exploited the features of bioisosteric triazoles to deliver a
family of benzamides with ample scope and functional group
tolerance, even in the presence of challenging boronate esters
or nitriles. The triazole could be removed in a traceless fashion,
leading to biorelevant compounds.
